easy.explanation: Verse 1 says that honour is not fitting for a fool.
easy.q: For whom is honour not seemly?

easy.explanation: Like a wandering bird, a causeless curse shall not come to its intended target.
easy.q: What will a causeless curse not do?

easy.explanation: Verse 6 warns that sending a message by the hand of a fool brings damage.
easy.q: By whose hand is it dangerous to send a message?

answers: Sometimes answering makes one like the fool, but at other times an answer prevents him from thinking himself wise
A fool must always be agreed with
People should never speak to fools
medium.explanation: Verses 4–5 give two contrasting principles: do not imitate the fool’s folly, but answer when silence would leave him wise in his own conceit.
medium.q: Why do the proverbs give two different instructions about answering a fool?

medium.explanation: The unequal legs of the lame are compared with a proverb in the mouth of fools, showing that it does not function properly.
medium.q: What does the comparison with the lame man’s legs teach about a proverb in a fool’s mouth?

answers: Both are improper and may be useless or harmful
medium.explanation: Honouring a fool is as misplaced and dangerous as binding a stone in a sling.
medium.q: What is common to giving honour to a fool and binding a stone in a sling?

answers: It has no proper destination and does not settle on its intended victim
challenge.explanation: As a bird wanders and a swallow flies, a causeless curse shall not come.
challenge.q: What does the picture of a wandering bird teach about a causeless curse?

answers: The message may be mishandled and bring damage
The message will be delivered too quickly
challenge.explanation: The fool is an unreliable messenger who may cause harm instead of accomplishing the task.
challenge.q: What danger is described in sending a message by the hand of a fool?

answers: He repeatedly returns to his folly
challenge.explanation: The comparison emphasizes the fool’s repeated return to the same foolish behavior.
challenge.q: What does the dog returning to its vomit teach about a fool?

paragraphs.title: The Lazy Person and His Excuses

easy.explanation: The slothful man says, “There is a lion in the way; a lion is in the streets.”
easy.q: What danger does the slothful man claim is in the way?

easy.explanation: The verse compares his movement on his bed to a door turning on its hinges.
easy.q: Where does the slothful man turn like a door upon its hinges?

easy.explanation: He hides his hand in his bosom and finds it grievous to bring it again to his mouth.
easy.q: What does the slothful man find difficult to bring back to his mouth?

answers: He invents dangers in the way
He asks a friend for help
medium.explanation: He uses the claim of a lion in the way as an excuse for staying inside.
medium.q: How does the slothful man avoid going out?

answers: He puts his hand into his clothing or lap and will not readily use it
medium.explanation: The expression describes his unwillingness even to complete the simple action of eating.
medium.q: What does it mean that the slothful man hides his hand in his bosom?

answers: His boast of wisdom conflicts with his lazy behavior
Both prove that he is an excellent adviser
Both show that he works diligently
medium.explanation: Although he considers himself wiser than seven men who can give a reason, his conduct reveals extreme laziness.
medium.q: What connection is made between the slothful man’s conduct and his opinion of himself?

answers: To show that he is brave
To show that he seeks a reason to avoid action
To show that he guards the streets
challenge.explanation: The imagined lion functions as an excuse for refusing to go out.
challenge.q: What is the purpose of the slothful man’s lion excuse?

answers: His laziness affects even the simplest action
He does not know how to eat
He has worked for a long time
challenge.explanation: The exaggerated description highlights the depth of his unwillingness to act.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the slothful man’s difficulty in bringing his hand to his mouth?

answers: He claims wisdom, but his conduct reveals laziness and inaction
He goes out but remains at home
challenge.explanation: He is wise in his own conceit, yet his behavior is marked by laziness rather than sound judgment.
challenge.q: What central contradiction appears in the slothful man?

paragraphs.title: Dangerous Interference and Deception Disguised as Play

easy.explanation: Verse 17 describes one who meddles with strife belonging to someone else.
easy.q: What does a person meddle with when it does not belong to him?

easy.explanation: Taking a dog by the ears is used as a picture of dangerous interference.
easy.q: What does the dangerous person take hold of?

easy.explanation: He attempts to excuse his conduct by saying, “Am not I in sport?”
easy.q: What does the man claim after deceiving or harming his neighbour?

answers: It can involve the meddler in someone else’s conflict
medium.explanation: The proverb compares such meddling with taking hold of a dog’s ears, an action likely to provoke harm.
medium.q: Why is meddling in another person’s strife dangerous?

answers: He inserts himself into another person’s quarrel
medium.explanation: The phrase describes entering a conflict that is not one’s own responsibility.
medium.q: What does “meddleth with strife belonging not to him” mean?

answers: A harmful act does not become harmless merely because it is called a game
Arrows are used only for entertainment
medium.explanation: The proverb rejects the excuse that serious harm is harmless simply because the offender calls it play.
medium.q: What connection is made between casting firebrands, arrows, and death and claiming to be in sport?

answers: Both actions may provoke a dangerous response
challenge.explanation: The image illustrates the danger of unnecessarily entering a volatile situation.
challenge.q: What is the connection between taking a dog by the ears and meddling in strife?

answers: It may cause real and serious harm
challenge.explanation: These images show that the supposed game can inflict genuine injury and death.
challenge.q: What do “firebrands, arrows, and death” reveal about an action described as sport?

answers: He must recognize that calling it play does not erase the harm
The injured person must always ignore it
challenge.explanation: The verse shows that a claim of sport does not excuse deceptive or destructive behavior.
challenge.q: What moral responsibility applies to someone who harms another and then says he was joking?

easy.explanation: The passage compares strife with a fire that continues while it is fed.
Verse 20 says, “Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out.”
easy.q: What happens when there is no wood?

answers: A way to prevent every quarrel
easy.explanation: The words of a talebearer are compared with wounds that go down into the innermost parts.
easy.q: What are the words of a talebearer like?

answers: Removing the talebearer and stopping the fuel of conflict
medium.explanation: When there is no wood or talebearer to feed the conflict, the fire and strife cease.
medium.q: What is required for strife to cease according to these verses?

answers: A person who spreads words that stir conflict
medium.explanation: The talebearer is presented as one who supplies fuel for strife.
medium.q: What is a talebearer in this passage?

answers: He feeds and kindles strife as fuel feeds a fire
medium.explanation: A contentious man adds material that causes a quarrel to burn more intensely.
medium.q: How does the comparison with coals and wood explain the contentious man?

answers: Strife can continue when people keep supplying it with fuel
Strife does not depend on speech
challenge.explanation: The comparison emphasizes that quarrels continue when contentious words and people keep feeding them.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from comparing fire with strife?

answers: To show that they remain superficial
To emphasize that they penetrate deeply and cause inward hurt
challenge.explanation: The expression portrays the deep emotional effect of harmful words.
challenge.q: Why are the words of a talebearer said to go down into the innermost parts of the belly?

answers: Removing the fuel can quiet strife, but the talebearer’s words still wound deeply
Both say that strife always grows
One verse concerns laziness and the other honor
challenge.explanation: The passage shows both how conflict can cease and how damaging words can continue to injure people inwardly.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between the image of fire going out and the words of a talebearer?

easy.explanation: Burning lips and a wicked heart are compared with a potsherd covered with silver dross.
easy.q: What is associated with burning lips?

easy.explanation: The hating person dissimulates with his lips and lays up deceit within him.
easy.q: What does the hating person hide?

easy.explanation: Verse 26 says that the wickedness shall be shown before the whole congregation.
easy.q: Where will the wickedness of hidden hatred eventually be shown?

answers: There may be seven abominations in his heart
A pleading voice is always false
No one should listen to anyone
medium.explanation: The verse warns that outwardly fair speech may conceal many abominations within the heart.
medium.q: Why should a person not immediately believe the fair speech of the one described here?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes striking outward speech contrasted with an evil heart.
medium.q: What does “burning lips” suggest in this context?

answers: Smooth or flattering speech may conceal hatred and deceit
medium.explanation: The passage warns about the difference between pleasant words and evil intentions.
medium.q: What contrast between outward appearance and inward reality appears in these verses?

answers: People should examine character and actions rather than speech alone
No one should ever be trusted
Only a loud voice is reliable
challenge.explanation: The passage shows that attractive speech can conceal deceit and hatred.
challenge.q: What does the command not to believe fair speech teach?

answers: The person’s wickedness is revealed publicly
challenge.explanation: Although hatred may be covered by deceit, the wickedness is eventually shown before the congregation.
challenge.q: How is concealed hatred finally exposed?

answers: The abundance or completeness of the evil hidden in the heart
challenge.explanation: The number stresses the many abominations concealed within the person.
challenge.q: What does the number seven emphasize in “seven abominations”?

easy.explanation: The proverb says that whoever digs a pit shall fall into it himself.
easy.q: Who may fall into the pit that he digs?

easy.explanation: The stone is said to return upon the one who rolled it.
easy.q: To whom will the rolling stone return?

easy.explanation: Verse 28 says that a flattering mouth worketh ruin.
easy.q: What does a flattering mouth work?

answers: The harm a person creates may return and injure him
medium.explanation: Both images teach that destructive schemes can rebound upon their maker.
medium.q: What common idea is shown by the pit and the stone?

answers: A mouth that does not speak
medium.explanation: A flattering mouth uses pleasant-sounding words that deceive and bring ruin.
medium.q: What does “a flattering mouth” mean in this context?

answers: False and flattering speech can produce hatred and ruin
medium.explanation: The verse links a lying tongue and a flattering mouth with hatred, affliction, and ruin.
medium.q: How are lying, hatred, and flattering speech connected in the final verse?

answers: A person may face the consequences of his own actions
Only other people are responsible for harm
challenge.explanation: The image of the stone returning shows that planned harm may come back upon the person who caused it.
challenge.q: What does the returning stone teach about personal responsibility?

answers: Both warn that concealed or directed evil eventually produces harm
They remove the danger of lying
challenge.explanation: The chapter ends by showing that deceitful and wicked actions bring destructive consequences.
challenge.q: How do the final verses connect with the earlier warning about deceit?

answers: Pleasant-sounding speech is not necessarily true or good
challenge.explanation: The verse warns that smooth speech can conceal falsehood and lead to hatred and ruin.
challenge.q: What conclusion follows from joining “a lying tongue” with “a flattering mouth”?
